item.content:encoded:
Even the biggest of homers couldn’t predict just how dominant Cam Schlittler would be this season. The ace of the New York Yankees has cemented himself as one of the top pitchers in all of baseball and proven that last year was not a fluke. Schlittler’s 2026 season may even go down as one of the best pitching performances in the entire history of the franchise. Despite the Yankees’ storied franchise, only six pitchers have won the Cy Young award for the team. Schlittler is likely about to change that.
With 6.0 fWAR accumulated throughout the 2026 season, Schlittler is tied with Milwaukee Brewers’ sensation Jacob Misiorowski for the league lead among pitchers. It’s no coincidence that both hurlers are the favorites to take home the Cy Young in their respective leagues. For Schlittler, he’d not only be the seventh Yankees pitcher to win the award, but he’d also be the youngest.
As the Yankees prepare for another postseason run, they will hope that Schlittler’s historic performance is able to carry over into October. As history has taught us, the Yankees win when their pitchers win.
Yankees Complete History of Cy Young Award Winners
It’s hard to fathom that the Yankees only average a Cy Young award winner every 20 years or so. From Mike Mussina to CC Sabathia, the franchise has certainly featured plenty of Hall of Fame pitchers that have come close to winning the award. Mussina was overshadowed by teammate Roger Clemens during his stellar 2001 campaign with the Yankees. Sabathia got as close to third place in the voting following his 2010 season.
Even the great Mariano Rivera couldn’t quite do enough to sway the voters and win the elusive award as a reliever. He finished in the top three of voting four separate times. This includes two seasons when he finished in the top 10 of the MVP race. It’s rare, but pitchers have occasionally made strong cases for MVP.
We’ll detail the six previous Yankees who actually managed to cross the finish line and why they deserved to take home the top pitching award. And because a Yankees season isn’t complete without a World Series title, we’ll also note how far a Cy Young winner got the team in the postseason.
Gerrit Cole, 2023
As the most recent Yankees pitcher to win the award, Gerrit Cole did something in 2023 that only one other player had accomplished in the team’s history, winning the award by unanimous decision. With all 30 first place votes, Cole more than doubled the amount of points that second-place pitcher Sonny Gray received.
As you might imagine, Cole’s 2023 is his most impressive season with the Yankees since joining the club in 2020. He struck out 222 hitters across 209 innings pitched. Although his 3.16 FIP doesn’t scream “elite pitcher,” he allowed just 157 hits while surrendering just 48 walks.
Despite Cole’s brilliance, the club finished with a mediocre 82-80 record, missing out on the playoffs for the first time since the 2016 season, though you couldn’t blame Cole for that. He boasted a 1.03 ERA and a minuscule 0.686 WHIP over his last five starts of the season, including a two-hit shutdown against the Toronto Blue Jays in his last start of the season. If only Aaron Judge hadn't run toe-first into the wall at Dodger Stadium.
Roger Clemens, 2001
As mentioned earlier, Clemens scooped away a lot of votes from Mussina when he won the Cy Young in 2001. Some would argue that Clemens probably stole that award, but you can’t deny that he still had a very good season.
With more emphasis placed on individual wins back then, Clemens boasted 20 wins to go alongside his 213 strikeouts. Clemens’ 2001 season would probably be considered his weakest of his seven award-winning seasons. But hey, it was the early 2000s. People voted more on vibes than actual performance.
Clemens’ 3.29 FIP that season was enough to help take the Yankees to the World Series, where they lost in heartbreaking fashion to the Arizona Diamondbacks. But we don’t have to dwell on that part.
Ron Guidry, 1978
Before Clemens won the award in 2001, it had been 23 years since a Yankees pitcher won it. But oh man, did Ron Guidry ever earn the award in 1978. With a 1.74 ERA across 273 1/3 innings pitched, his season is what many consider to be the best by a pitcher in team history. His home run per nine rate of 0.4 is almost laughable.
Even by modern metrics, Guidry was the clear-cut winner that season. His 2.19 FIP and 208 ERA+ was leaps and bounds better than any other pitcher up for consideration that year, which is why he became the first Yankees pitcher to win the award unanimously.
Guidry was a large reason that the team won 100 games that year. The Yankees would carry that tremendous momentum into the postseason and defeat the Los Angeles Dodgers in the World Series.
Sparky Lyle, 1977
Unlike the long wait in between Clemens and Guidry winning the Cy Young, the Yankees actually had quite the time in the late 70s when it came to award-winning pitchers. Before Guidry, the team saw reliever Sparky Lyle take home the award in 1977. He became just the second reliever in MLB history to win the honor. Since then, seven more relievers have joined the rare club.
When looking at his numbers, you probably wouldn’t really consider Lyle to be a dominant force out of the bullpen. Despite that, he was certainly one of the most effective pitchers in the league. With just 68 strikeouts in 137 innings, Lyle didn’t just rely on swing and misses to get outs. He collected 13 wins and 26 saves, demonstrating just how pivotal he was to the Yankees.
With Lyle coming out of the pen, the Yankees won 100 games in the regular season. He then helped pave the way to a World Series title over the Dodgers.
Whitey Ford, 1961
With 236 career wins and six World Series rings in his collection, Whitey Ford is one of the foremost Yankees winners in team history. In 1961, he added a Cy Young to his trophy case. At 32 years old, he threw a career-high 283 innings, which included 11 complete games and three shutouts.
Ford’s 1961 season may be outshined in the annals of history by Roger Maris’ record-setting performance, but that doesn’t make it any less impressive. Like other pitchers on this list, Ford didn’t put up mind-boggling numbers or boast off-the-charts metrics. Outside of innings pitched, he didn’t really do one thing extremely well. However, he did do just about everything very well.
Ford was more than enough of a pitcher to be considered the ace of a team that some argue to be one of the best teams in MLB history. With 109 wins and a World Series title, it is hard to argue against that claim.
Bob Turley, 1958
Just three years before Ford won his Cy Young, Bob Turley became the first Yankees pitcher to win the award in 1958. Once again, like a number of other Yankees on this list, Turley’s 1958 season isn’t something that you would circle as an all-time great year. His 4.04 WHIP and 119 ERA+ were shockingly poor in hindsight.
Turley probably became the first Yankees pitcher to steal the award from a more deserving pitcher as well. Sorry, Warren Spahn. While Turley threw 245 1/3 innings, including 19 complete games, he was an especially wild pitcher. Turley walked 128 batters, nearly double the amount of walks surrendered by the second and third place pitchers in the Cy Young voting combined that year.
With all of that said, Turley pitched well enough to help lead the Yankees to 92 wins. They then went on to defeat the Milwaukee Braves in seven games in the World Series. When all is said and done, what more could you ask for?

item.content:encoded:
That's what he is doing now, he's supporting Gary Sanchez, Miguel Andujar and last but not least Anthony Volpe, read more HERE. These guys were given "labels" from the fan base, which happens a lot when you don't meet expectations underneath New York's bright lights. For years we have been writing about how the Yankees coddle their players and but now CC wants the Yankees to also help them adapt to this demanding environment.
I agree with that to a point. New York is a tough place to play for established veterans, let alone when you are a young kid like Volpe was making it onto the big stage as an everyday player. There should be some mental preparation there for players, but it should also be prepared with the confidence of pairing that with good fundamentals to help you perform at a high level under those bright lights. If you have that track record of faltering (like Volpe has) that's when the Yankees need to be more hands on. It's exactly what the Yankees haven't done well.
Everyone in life needs feedback. It's what helps us improve and hone in on our craft. The Yankees do need to look for new ways to help guys deal with the pressures in the bright lights but maybe that doesn't look like what CC is suggesting. Maybe it's a more real-world scenario that the rest of us deal with since we don't make the big bucks playing a kid's game for a living.
The Yankees coddle; I call it the Aaron Boone approach. He's warm and fuzzy. The Bronx, however, is not a warm and fuzzy place. It's as real as it gets. Why aren't we giving that fair, but realistic approach to these guys? This isn't a sunshine and rainbows environment. This isn't a "safe space." This is a 'pull your big boy pants up and be tough' environment and get the job done. Figure it out and use your resources. The Yankees have lots of resources and patience. The fans don't have the patience, and we shouldn't be expected to have patience.
You can still give honest feedback that is firm but fair. It builds character. Hugs are not included on the side here. That's what Boone and the Yankees do. They give hugs, but they don't give reality. Give these guys a real environment to adapt in and help them through the bumps and they will perform better, period. If they don't, then they get sent down to the minors like Volpe did or traded. 
Only the strong survive here, and the Yankees need to figure that out. The coddling isn't working. Not everyone is cut out to play here so it's time to be honest about that.

item.content:encoded:
Baseball Hall of Fame pitcher and legendary New York Yankees starter CC Sabathia has told the story many times: Dave Stewart changed his mindset forever at just 9 years old in his hometown Vallejo, California.
Stewart, a three-time World Series champion and World Series MVP during his time pitching for the Oakland Athletics, made a surprise visit to Sabathia’s Boys and Girls Club when he was just a kid. Stewart shared a message of inspiration, and it’s one that stuck with a fellow African American major league great who just so happened to hoist his own World Series trophy in a town known best for their hardware on the diamond.
It’s hard to become a Yankees legend, and it’s even harder to find your name amongst the rarest of rare in Monument Park, where the likes of Mickey Mantle, Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig reside in immortality. On Sept. 26, Sabathia will have his No. 52 retired forever by one of the most iconic franchises in sports, an honor he can’t wait to finally see come to life after learning the shocking news months prior.
But while Sabathia’s on-field accomplishments are Hall of Fame and Monument Park worthy, his off-the-field contributions to the next generation are just as timeless and important.
That was on full display Monday at Alpine Country Club in New Jersey, where Sabathia held his 6th Annual Golf Classic for his PitCCh In Foundation. With golf being his latest sports passion post-retirement, it’s a day Sabathia looks forward to with his friends while making a community impact that feels as good as hitting a hole-in-one.
"It’s always fun to be able to get out on the golf course and obviously raise money for a good cause," he told FOX Business before teeing off alongside the likes of Victor Cruz, Gary Sheffield, JR Smith, Matt Barnes, Ron Harper, Jimmy Rollins, Ja Rule and the list goes on. "Our foundation, the money goes directly to the kids in the Bronx. Our kids back home in our hometown of Vallejo [California], this is a direct effect of people coming out here to play golf.
"I was just sitting down talking to Adam Jones and talking about being able to play golf, and the last six years, the network I’ve been able to build just around the game of golf. I wish I would’ve been playing longer, but I’m here now and excited."
The event raised more than $450,000 to help PitCCh In continue creating opportunities and resources for young people and their families on both coasts in one unforgettable day.
It’s moments like this that have Sabathia excited for this next chapter of his life. Yes, he will still be impacting the game of baseball, whether that be broadcasting, or working with the Yankees and MLB as a whole.
But his foundation is something he holds near and dear to his heart, as does his wife Amber and their four children. In fact, PitCCh In is a true part of the family in their eyes.
"It’s great to see the foundation thriving in retirement. Sometimes in retirement, foundations go by the wayside, or players get busy and different things happen. But this is kind of our fifth child we’ve always said," he said, smiling. "PitCCh In has been such a huge part of not just our lives, but like we said, kids on both coasts [and] our kids’ lives.
"I was just with Derek [Jeter] and he celebrated his 30 years for Turn 2 [Foundation], and just the impact he’s been able to make on the youth just in general. So many different stories, Jeter’s Leaders [Program] and people, in the last 30 years that he’s been able to impact. Hopefully, PitCCh In can continue to be that vehicle for years to come, too."
PitCCh In has done everything from field renovations to baseball clinics, to providing college scholarships and school supplies as ways to impact the communities the Sabathia family cares about most. They also have a mentorship program where, through educational and athletic activities, the lives of the youth involved are strengthened on levels both physical and emotional.
Sabathia’s baseball legacy will be told forever in the halls in Cooperstown and behind the center field wall at Yankee Stadium come Sept. 26. But his story is one that goes well beyond the baseball player.
It’s also the person he is, and the family he’s surrounded by, that continues to support and impact in a way he felt from the very beginning.
"It was big for me when I was a kid, just having people that took interest in my life," he said. "I just think about me being lucky in the situation I was in, whether it was my Boys and Girls Club – there was a guy named Philmore Graham who ran my Boys and Girls Club and took a huge interest in me. My high school baseball coach, my fifth grade teacher, all these different people who made an impact and why I’m sitting here. I want to hopefully be that for a kid."

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — Dentro de unas semanas, CC Sabathia, uno de los lanzadores más laureados de su época, verá cómo su número se alza en la valla del exterior del Yankee Stadium, para siempre e intocable. Los Yankees le dieron un título en su primera temporada y una placa para despedir su carrera.
Así que, cuando la leyenda de los Yankees habla de lo que significa para un jugador llevar esa camiseta a rayas, la gente de la organización suele prestarle atención.
Y lo que dijo esta semana no fue precisamente una celebración. Fue una advertencia, expresada sin rodeos, sobre cómo trata la franquicia a sus jóvenes promesas.
El ambiente era informal, una jornada benéfica de golf en Nueva Jersey. El mensaje, en cambio, no lo era. Tocaba un tema sobre el que los aficionados de los Yankees llevan años discutiendo sin que ningún pilar de la franquicia se atreviera a dar su nombre al respecto.
CC Sabathia, cuyo dorsal número 52 se retirará y cuya placa en el Monument Park se inaugurará antes del partido de los Yankees del 26 de septiembre contra los Orioles de Baltimore, dijo que el equipo debe esforzarse más para proteger a sus jugadores jóvenes de la enorme presión que conllevan las expectativas en Nueva York.
En declaraciones a OutKick durante el sexto torneo anual de golf de su fundación PitCCh In, celebrado el lunes en el Alpine Country Club, este lanzador zurdo del Salón de la Fama mencionó a Anthony Volpe y George Lombard Jr. como ejemplos positivos, y a los exjugadores de los Yankees Gary Sánchez y Miguel Andújar como ejemplos a evitar.
El núcleo de su argumento es que a los jugadores del Bronx se les etiqueta antes de que tengan la oportunidad de crecer. Una mala racha se convierte en una etiqueta. La etiqueta se queda pegada. Y una carrera puede definirse por su peor etapa en lugar de por su potencial.
Una crítica dirigida al entorno de los Yankees, no a los jugadores
Sabathia tuvo cuidado de plantear el tema como un fallo de preparación, no como una crítica al talento. Argumentó que los Yankees no pueden eliminar la presión del mercado, pero sí pueden enseñar a los jugadores sin experiencia cómo lidiar con ella.
Contó cómo veía cómo a los jóvenes de los Yankees les encasillaban casi nada más llegar, y destacó una excepción evidente. Para ilustrar su argumento, Sabathia explicó por qué Aaron Judge nunca se vio envuelto en la misma trampa.
«Como es de aquí, quiere hacerlo bien. Y es que he visto a un montón de jugadores jóvenes de los Yankees, ya sea Gary Sánchez, Miguel Andújar o quien sea: te ponen una etiqueta y ya está, lo cual es un rollo, sobre todo para un jugador joven. Creo que el único jugador joven que llegó y lo hizo bien fue Judge, porque bateó 50 jonrones y todo el mundo dejó de meterse con él. Así que es difícil ganarte el respeto de la afición cuando eres tan joven», dijo Sabathia.
A continuación, relacionó esa tendencia directamente con la mala racha defensiva de Lombard y con lo que él considera que es responsabilidad de los Yankees.
«A George Lombard Jr. le acaba de pasar lo mismo. Cometió seis errores seguidos y ya empezaste a oír quejas y todo tipo de comentarios. Así que es difícil crecer aquí como jugador joven y creo que los Yankees tienen que esforzarse más por proteger a estos chicos y ayudarles a entender lo que significa vestir la camiseta a rayas. Habrá altibajos, tienes que hacer caso omiso de los rumores y salir a jugar al béisbol todos los días», dijo Sabathia.
Volpe y Lombard exponen el argumento en tiempo real
El momento elegido ilustra perfectamente lo que dice Sabathia. Pocos jugadores han vivido tan de cerca los altibajos de Nueva York esta temporada como Volpe.
El jugador de 25 años, que en su día fue considerado la apuesta propia de los Yankees para el puesto de shortstop, fue enviado a la Triple A de Scranton/Wilkes-Barre tras el partido de los Yankees del 3 de agosto, lo que dejó el camino libre para George Lombard Jr., la mayor promesa del club. Volpe no volvió hasta más de un mes después, y solo cuando Jazz Chisholm Jr. se lesionó el pulgar.
Cuando por fin volvió el 10 de septiembre, el novato de los Yankees respondió de la mejor manera posible. Jugando en una nueva posición, la segunda base, Volpe conectó un grand slam e impulsó cinco carreras —su mejor marca personal— en la victoria por 10-3 sobre Colorado, y luego salió a saludar al público mientras los aficionados coreaban su nombre. Acabó con 3 de 4 y una base robada. Fue su segundo grand slam de su carrera en la temporada regular, que se suma al que bateó en la Serie Mundial de 2024.
El debut de Lombard con los New York Yankees fue todo lo contrario. Este jugador de 21 años conectó un jonrón en su primer hit en las Grandes Ligas durante su debut el 4 de agosto y estuvo a la altura durante dos semanas, cometiendo solo un error en sus primeros 14 partidos.
Entonces empezaron a llover los errores. Lombard cometió un error en seis partidos seguidos a finales de agosto, igualando un récord de la franquicia de los Yankees que solo había logrado antes Chick Fewster en 1921. Según la Elias Sports Bureau, fue la racha más larga de este tipo en las Grandes Ligas desde que Mark Lewis, de Cleveland, cometiera errores en siete partidos seguidos en 1992. El entrenador de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, siguió apoyándole públicamente, pero las quejas que describió Sabathia ya habían empezado.
¿Por qué la advertencia te afecta más ahora?
La crítica de Sabathia llega en un momento clave para la plantilla. Los Yankees dependen cada vez más de jugadores de la cantera, con contratos asequibles, para respaldar a un núcleo de veteranos muy caros. A Lombard, Spencer Jones, Ben Rice y Cam Schlittler se les está pidiendo que asuman una responsabilidad importante cuando aún están en los inicios de sus carreras.
Esto aumenta la presión sobre el sistema de cantera de los Yankees. Ya no se trata solo de formar a jóvenes promesas. Se trata de ayudarles a sobrevivir al «referéndum» diario que supone jugar en el Bronx, donde cada error y cada decisión sobre la alineación se convierte en tema de conversación.
Sabathia dejó claro que sigue confiando en Volpe, aunque reconoció la incómoda verdad de que puede que los mejores años de este jugador de los Yankees no lleguen en Nueva York.
«Si piensas en la perseverancia y la determinación de Volpe, ¿qué otra cosa va a hacer? No va a tirar la toalla», dijo Sabathia. «Esto es lo que ha querido hacer toda su vida. Siempre ha querido jugar al béisbol, y ha pasado por situaciones difíciles. El béisbol es un deporte duro, pero creo que seguro que lo hará mejor, ya sea jugando de segunda base, de campocorto en el Bronx o en cualquier otro sitio».
Concluyó diciendo que la presión en este deporte es única, y puso como ejemplo al novato de Boston, Roman Anthony, para ilustrar su argumento.
«Esto solo pasa aquí. Si piensas en cualquier otro sitio, en ningún otro lugar ocurre algo así. Piensa en lo que está pasando Roman Anthony en Boston. Si eso pasara aquí en Nueva York, sería noticia principal en Sportscenter todos los días», añadió Sabathia. «Es otra historia cuando te pones la camiseta a rayas».
Las cifras que hay detrás de lo que dice Sabathia
Los datos le dan fuerza a su argumento. No se trata simplemente de la queja de un veterano. La posición de shortstop lo dice todo por sí sola.
La temporada pasada, Volpe fue el campocorto de la Liga Americana que más errores cometió, con 19, y eso que jugó los últimos cuatro meses con un desgarro en el labrum del hombro, un detalle que cambia la perspectiva con la que se valoró su defensa en aquel momento. Esta temporada, antes incluso de que ascendieran a Lombard, los campocortos de los Yankees habían sumado entre todos 16 errores, según las cifras citadas por ESPN. Lombard registró entonces un porcentaje de fildeo de 0,925 en sus primeros partidos, con siete errores en sus primeros 20 encuentros.
Esas cifras reflejan exactamente la trampa que describe Sabathia. Un jugador joven de los Yankees hereda un puesto que ya está en el punto de mira, comete un error evidente y se convierte en el centro de todas las miradas. El contexto —una lesión un año, la curva de aprendizaje de un chico de 21 años al siguiente— suele perderse entre tanto revuelo.
La propia trayectoria de Sabathia pone de relieve el contraste que él mismo está señalando. Este icono de los Yankees llegó a las Grandes Ligas con 20 años, en el Cleveland de 2001, y sintió la presión de inmediato, pero ha dicho que llegar a Nueva York en 2009 fue una experiencia totalmente diferente. Respondió a esa presión ayudando a conseguir el 27.º título de la Serie Mundial en su primera temporada, el último campeonato de la franquicia.
Los Yankees no han vuelto a la cima desde entonces, y solo llegaron a una Serie Mundial, en 2024, antes de caer derrotados ante los Dodgers de Los Ángeles. Ahora que el equipo se ha asegurado otra plaza en la postemporada y Volpe intenta recuperar su prestigio mientras Lombard se adapta en su primer mes, la leyenda de la franquicia no tiene que ir muy lejos para defender su postura. La gran incógnita de cara a octubre es si la organización se tomará en serio este argumento.
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

item.content:encoded:
It’s been said many times over a century: earning your pinstripes with the New York Yankees is one of the hardest things to do in baseball.
Just take Anthony Volpe’s rollercoaster career with the ballclub, which has once again become a storyline as they head toward the postseason. Through four seasons, Volpe, a former first-round pick by the Yankees, has been showered with cheers, vitriol and everything in between from the fan base whose expectations will never fall lower than World Series or bust.
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
If that’s not hard for a 25-year-old to deal with, Hall of Fame left-hander CC Sabathia was even a bit intimidated by the weight the pinstripes hold when he was a free agent in 2009. He eventually signed on and became a beloved figure in Yankees lore — his No. 52 is set to be retired on Sept. 26 — but he understands it’s not for everybody.
While speaking at his PitCCh In Foundation’s 6th Annual Golf Classic at Alpine Country Club on Monday, Sabathia suggested to OutKick that the Yankees should come up with a way to not coddle those young players from the expectations, but rather help ease their way into it.
"It’s hard to watch, right?" he said when asked about what Volpe has gone through, especially now that he’s hearing cheers again after performing well following his latest call-up. "Because he’s from here, he wants to do well. And I just watched so many young players for the Yankees, whether it’s Gary Sanchez, whether it was Miguel Andujar, whoever it is, you get a label and that’s what it is, which sucks especially for a young player. I feel like the only young player that came in and did well was [Aaron] Judge because he hit 50 homers and everybody was off his back. So, it’s hard to build up equity with the fan base when you’re so young.
"George Lombard [Jr.] just went through the same thing. He had six errors in a row, and you started hearing grumblings and all these different things. So, it’s hard to develop here as a young player and I think the Yankees need to do a better job to insulating these guys and helping them understand what it is to put on the pinstripes. There’s going to be ups and downs, you gotta cancel out the noise and go out and play baseball every single day."
Of course, it’s easier said than done in a New York market where championships, no matter the sport, are expected each time a season begins. But the only way through is forward for players like Volpe, whose ups and downs since reaching the big leagues have kept fans guessing. They see what could be, but consistency hasn’t been there for the highly touted prospect.
"You think about Volpe’s perseverance and determination — what else is he going to do? He’s not going to quit," Sabathia added. "This is what he wanted to do his whole life. He wanted to play baseball his whole life, and he’s been in tough situations. Baseball is a hard game, but I think he’ll be better for sure, whether he’s playing second base, whether he’s playing shortstop in the Bronx or somewhere else.
"Wherever it is, he’s talented enough to play the game. Hopefully he can do some things well and help us down the stretch. Jazz can get healthy, they can platoon. We’ll see what happens. But I’m super excited for his future, not only here but if it’s somewhere else, too."
Sabathia spent 19 years in the major leagues, where expectation was immediate for him as well coming up with the Cleveland Indians in 2001 as a 20-year-old. He felt that pressure there, and even for the half season he played with the Milwaukee Brewers.
But arriving in New York was a different story in 2009. Sabathia and the rest of his star teammates came through, though, winning the World Series that season and giving a franchise synonymous with titles its 27th to extend the MLB record.
Since then, the Yankees haven’t been able to add their 28th, making just one Fall Classic in 2024 before falling to the Los Angeles Dodgers. Sabathia hopes this could be the year the Yankees get back and see it all the way through so his squad isn’t still the last New York team to win it all.
But then again, the pressure is immense to make that happen. It’s already begun as the Yankees clinch yet another postseason berth and the chance to hoist the trophy at the end of the season.
It’s pressure Sabathia feels is found nowhere else in MLB, especially for young players trying to make a name for themselves on one of the most iconic sports franchises in the world.
"This is the only place it happens. If you think about anywhere else, it doesn’t happen anywhere else. You think about what Roman Anthony is going through in Boston. If that was here in New York, it would be leading Sportscenter every single day," Sabathia said.
"It's a different beast when you put on the pinstripes."

item.content:encoded:
Se ha dicho muchas veces a lo largo de un siglo: ganarse la camiseta a rayas de los New York Yankees es una de las cosas más difíciles de conseguir en el béisbol.
Fíjate, por ejemplo, en Anthony la carrera llena de altibajos de Volpe en el equipo, que ha vuelto a ser tema de conversación ahora que se acercan a la postemporada. A lo largo de cuatro temporadas, Volpe, un exjugador elegido en primera ronda por los Yankees, ha recibido tanto vítores como críticas feroces y todo lo que hay entre medias por parte de una afición cuyas expectativas nunca bajarán de «la Serie Mundial o nada».
Esta página puede contener enlaces de afiliados a socios de apuestas deportivas legales. Si te registras o realizas una apuesta, FOX News podría recibir una compensación. Este contenido lo ha creado un equipo que trabaja de forma independiente de la redacción de FOX News.
Si eso ya es difícil de afrontar para alguien de 25 años, al lanzador zurdo del Salón de la Fama CC Sabathia incluso le intimidaba un poco el peso que tienen las rayas cuando era agente libre en 2009. Al final firmó y se convirtió en una figura muy querida en la historia de los Yankees —su dorsal n.º 52 se retirará el 26 de septiembre—, pero entiende que no es algo para todo el mundo.
Durante su intervención el lunes en la 6.ª edición anual del torneo « Golf Classic» de su fundación PitCCh In, celebrado en el Alpine Country Club, Sabathia le comentó a OutKick que los Yankees deberían encontrar una forma de no sobreproteger a esos jugadores jóvenes de las expectativas, sino más bien ayudarles a adaptarse poco a poco a ellas.
«Es duro de ver, ¿verdad?», dijo cuando le preguntaron por lo que ha pasado Volpe, sobre todo ahora que vuelve a oír vítores tras su buen rendimiento tras su última convocatoria. «Como es de aquí, quiere hacerlo bien. Y es que he visto a tantos jugadores jóvenes de los Yankees —ya sea Gary Sánchez, Miguel Andújar o quien sea— que te ponen una etiqueta y ya está, lo cual es un rollo, sobre todo para un jugador joven. Creo que el único jugador joven que llegó y lo hizo bien fue [Aaron] Judge, porque bateó 50 jonrones y todo el mundo dejó de meterse con él. Así que es difícil ganarte el respeto de la afición cuando eres tan joven».
«George Lombard [Jr.] acaba de pasar por lo mismo. Cometió seis errores seguidos y empezaron a oírse quejas y todo tipo de comentarios. Así que es difícil crecer aquí como jugador joven y creo que los Yankees tienen que esforzarse más por proteger a estos chicos y ayudarles a entender lo que significa vestir la camiseta a rayas. Habrá altibajos, tienes que ignorar los rumores y salir a jugar al béisbol todos los días».
Claro que es más fácil decirlo que hacerlo en un mercado como el de Nueva York, donde se esperan títulos, sea cual sea el deporte, cada vez que empieza una temporada. Pero el único camino es seguir adelante para jugadores como Volpe, cuyos altibajos desde que llegó a las grandes ligas han tenido a los aficionados en vilo. Ven lo que podría llegar a ser, pero a este prometedor jugador tan aclamado le ha faltado consistencia.
«Piensa en la perseverancia y la determinación de Volpe: ¿qué otra cosa va a hacer? No va a rendirse», añadió Sabathia. «Esto es lo que ha querido hacer toda su vida. Siempre ha querido jugar al béisbol, y ha pasado por situaciones difíciles. El béisbol es un deporte duro, pero creo que seguro que mejorará, tanto si juega de segunda base como si juega de campocorto en el Bronx o en cualquier otro sitio».
«Sea donde sea, tiene el talento suficiente para jugar. Ojalá pueda destacar en algunas cosas y echarnos una mano en la recta final. Los Jazz pueden recuperar a sus lesionados y hacer rotaciones. Ya veremos qué pasa. Pero estoy superilusionado con su futuro, no solo aquí, sino también si acaba en otro sitio».
Sabathia pasó 19 años en las Grandes Ligas, donde las expectativas sobre él fueron inmediatas desde que debutó con los Cleveland Indians en 2001, con solo 20 años. Sintió esa presión allí, e incluso durante la media temporada que jugó con los Brewers de Milwaukee .
Pero llegar a Nueva York en 2009 fue otra historia. Sin embargo, Sabathia y el resto de sus compañeros estrella estuvieron a la altura: ganaron la Serie Mundial esa temporada y le dieron a una franquicia sinónimo de títulos su 27.º título, ampliando así el récord de la « MLB ».
Desde entonces, los Yankees no han podido sumar su 28.º título, y solo llegaron a una Serie Mundial en 2024, donde cayeron ante los Dodgers de Los ÁngelesLos . Sabathia espera que este sea el año en que los Yankees vuelvan a la carga y lleguen hasta el final, para que su equipo deje de ser el último de Nueva York en ganar el título.
Pero, bueno, la presión para conseguirlo es enorme. Ya ha empezado, ahora que los Yankees se han asegurado otra clasificación para la postemporada y la oportunidad de levantar el trofeo al final de la temporada.
Es una presión que, según Sabathia, no se siente en ningún otro sitio de « MLB », sobre todo para los jugadores jóvenes que intentan hacerse un nombre en una de las franquicias deportivas más emblemáticas del mundo.
«Esto solo pasa aquí. Si piensas en cualquier otro sitio, en ningún otro sitio ocurre. Piensa en lo que está pasando Roman Anthony en Boston. Si eso pasara aquí en Nueva York, sería noticia principal en Sportscenter todos los días», dijo Sabathia.
«Es otra historia cuando te pones el uniforme a rayas».

item.content:encoded:
On Monday night, the New York Yankees are playing the first game of their series with the Minnesota Twins at Target Field.
They most recently won two out of three games against the New York Mets (in the Bronx).
UPDATE: The Yankees won 8-3.
Alex Rodriguez’s Former Yankees Teammate Still A Free Agent
With the season nearly over, it’s worth noting that a former Yankees pitcher (who recently became a free agent) is still available.
Chris Martin was released by the Texas Rangers last month.
MLB.com wrote (on August 8): “Texas Rangers released RHP Chris Martin.”
Martin is in the middle of his 11th season pitching at the MLB level.
He had gone 1-1 with a 9.00 ERA in 16 games for the Rangers this year.
Looking At Martin’s Yankees Stint
Martin (who is 40) was picked in the 21st round of the 2005 MLB Draft.
He spent his rookie year (2014) with the Colorado Rockies.
Ahead of the 2015 season, they traded him to the Yankees.
Martin appeared in 24 games for the Yankees that season.
He went 0-2 with a 5.66 ERA.
During that year, Martin got to be teammates with MLB legends such as Alex Rodriguez, Mark Teixeira and CC Sabathia.
Other Stops For Martin
In addition to the Rangers, Rockies and Yankees, Martin has also spent time with the Atlanta Braves, Boston Red Sox, Chicago Cubs and Los Angeles Dodgers.
The 2021 World Series Champion has gone 19-25 with a 3.53 ERA in 434 career games.
